content: For individuals living with multiple sclerosis, engaging in physical activity has been shown to enhance physical function, functional mobility, walking speed, endurance, cardiorespiratory fitness, strength, and balance. Studies have demonstrated that interventions lasting an average of 13 weeks can lead to improvements in strength, while dance-based interventions have been associated with better functional mobility and balance. In addition to physical health benefits, evidence suggests that physical activity can positively impact cognitive function in people with multiple sclerosis. Recent research indicates that aerobic exercise has a small but significant effect on physical, mental, and social aspects of health-related quality of life, including reductions in fatigue and depressive symptoms. For individuals with spinal cord injury, physical activity has been shown to improve walking function, muscular strength, and upper extremity function. It may also alleviate shoulder pain, enhance vascular function in paralyzed limbs, and improve health-related quality of life. In people with Parkinson’s disease, physical activity can improve motor symptoms, functional mobility, endurance, freezing of gait, and the speed of forward and backward movements. Emerging evidence also suggests that exercise may enhance global cognitive function in this population. For individuals with a history of stroke, physical activity has been shown to improve physical function, particularly upper limb function, sensory-motor function of the lower limb, balance, walking speed, distance, endurance, cardiorespiratory fitness, mobility, and activities of daily living. Evidence also suggests potential cognitive benefits from physical activity in this group. In adults with major clinical depression, physical activity has been shown to improve health-related quality of life. Similarly, for individuals with cognitive impairments, including schizophrenia, physical activity has demonstrated benefits for cognition, working memory, social cognition, and attention/vigilance. Moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity has been associated with significant improvements in health-related quality of life and reductions in disability. For children and adults with intellectual disabilities, physical activity has been shown to improve physical function, particularly balance and strength. Interventions lasting 6–24 weeks have reported significant improvements in static, dynamic, and combined static-dynamic balance compared to controls. In children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), evidence, including a review of randomized controlled trials, indicates that exercise is positively associated with improvements in attention, executive function, and social behaviors. The WHO guidelines emphasize that individuals living with disabilities can derive the same physiological health benefits from physical activity as the general population. Despite limited research specifically involving people with disabilities, expert opinion supports the inclusion of this population in general physical activity recommendations. The benefits of physical activity for individuals with disabilities are considered to outweigh potential harms. For children and adolescents living with disabilities, it is recommended to limit sedentary behavior, particularly recreational screen time, as higher levels of sedentary behavior are associated with poor health outcomes such as increased adiposity, poorer cardiometabolic health, reduced fitness, and shorter sleep duration. Similarly, adults living with disabilities are advised to minimize sedentary time, as it is linked to increased risks of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and type 2 diabetes. Replacing sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity, including light-intensity activity, provides health benefits. The WHO guidelines recommend that adults living with disabilities aim to exceed the recommended levels of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity to counteract the detrimental effects of high levels of sedentary behavior. For children, adolescents, and adults with disabilities, sedentary behavior is defined as time spent sitting or lying with low energy expenditure while awake, in contexts such as education, home, community settings, or transportation. The development of these recommendations involved a thorough assessment of the balance of benefits and harms, the certainty of evidence, and considerations of feasibility, acceptability, and health equity. Despite limited evidence on harms, expert opinion and available data suggest that the benefits of physical activity far outweigh the risks. The guidelines highlight that engaging in any amount of physical activity is better than none, and individuals not currently meeting the recommendations should be encouraged to start with small amounts of activity to gain health benefits.
